notes.b: A family function is something the family does for its members and for society. There are five: physical, economic, emotional, educational and social, and together they explain what a family is for.
points: The five functions are physical (bodily needs and protection), economic (income and spending), emotional (love and security), educational (passing on skills, language and values) and social (learning how to behave in society).
The emotional function is also called the nurturing or psychological function, and the social function is also called socialisation. The content is the same whichever name an exam uses.
Functions remain constant across societies even when family structures change, because every society still needs its members fed, supported, loved, taught and socialised.
Other social institutions can adopt a function (take it over) or supplement it (help the family with it). The State, through public services and payments, supports the family in each function.
One family activity may serve more than one function, so the categories overlap.
notes.tip: Social does not mean 'social life'. It means socialisation, learning the norms and values of society, so do not mix it up with the emotional function (love, security, self-esteem). State supports are not family functions: they supplement them.

notes.b: The physical function meets the basic bodily needs of family members and protects those who cannot protect themselves.
points: The family provides food, warmth, shelter, clothing, rest and a safe environment for its members.
Procreation (reproduction) ensures the continuation of the population and gives children their first physical home.
The family protects dependants who are vulnerable, including young children, older people, the sick and people with disabilities, because they cannot meet their own needs.

Other institutions supplement this function: local authority housing, GPs and the public health service (the HSE and its public health nurses), hospitals, school meals programmes, and foster care and Tusla (the Child and Family Agency, set up in 2014).

The State supports the physical function through the medical card (which helps with health costs for those eligible), housing supports from local authorities, home support services for older people (formerly called home help), public health nursing, Tusla's child protection and family support, and welfare payments towards living costs.
notes.tip: Procreation belongs to the physical function in the exam schemes (reproduction, survival of the species), not the emotional one. When you name a State support, say how it helps, for example the medical card helps with health costs, and name a different support for each function.

notes.b: The economic function provides the income that supports dependants and links the family to the wider economy.
points: Adults earn income to support dependants, meaning children and other dependent family members, because dependants cannot yet or cannot any longer support themselves.
Family members pay taxes and spend on goods and services, which supports the wider economy.
Managing the household budget means planning income and spending, and saving.
Historically, in Ireland and in some societies today, a large family worked together as an economic unit, such as a farm or family business, in which every member worked.
Banks, credit unions and insurance companies supplement the family's money management by offering savings, loans and cover against loss.
The Money Advice and Budgeting Service (MABS) helps families deal with debt and plan their budgets.

The State supports this function through social welfare payments such as Child Benefit, Jobseeker's payments, Carer's Allowance, disability payments, the Working Family Payment (formerly Family Income Supplement) and the State pension.
The State also eases family costs through the Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance, medical cards, free school books and the school meals programme.
notes.tip: The economic function is not 'the family has money'. It is earning to support dependants, paying taxes and spending. Do not name 'welfare payments' as the support for every function: pick a different support for each.

notes.b: The emotional function gives family members love, security and a sense of belonging, so that children grow into well-adjusted people.
points: A secure, loving home gives children the emotional base from which they develop self-esteem and learn to express emotions and discuss feelings.
Family members learn healthy relationships through daily contact with each other.
Parents act as role models and support each other emotionally, which helps children develop emotionally because they copy what they see.
Other sources supplement the family when it cannot meet emotional needs: school counsellors, youth services, bereavement and relationship counselling, parenting courses, friends and community groups.

The State supports this function through parenting courses and programmes, family support services and psychological services (HSE, Tusla), and by funding voluntary and community groups that provide counselling.
notes.tip: Keep this function about love, security and self-esteem. In exams, say what the home gives (a safe, secure home where children express feelings, parents as role models) and link any State support to how it helps.

notes.b: The educational function passes on knowledge, language and values informally from birth and prepares children for formal schooling.
points: The family is the primary educator (the first and main teacher), passing on beliefs, language, skills and customs through informal learning from birth.
Praise, encouragement and a stimulating environment promote early intellectual development.
Parents support formal school work through help with homework, reading together, educational outings and an interest in school, so that children reach their potential.
Pre-school, primary, second-level and third-level education take over formal teaching as the child grows, supplementing the family.
The State supports this function through the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) free pre-school scheme, free education in recognised schools, and the National Childcare Scheme.

Special needs support in schools includes resource hours, special classes, special needs assistants (SNAs) and exam accommodations. Third-level access schemes such as HEAR and DARE help students who might otherwise miss out.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the family as primary educator, passing on beliefs and customs, plus a named support such as the ECCE scheme, schools or special needs supports, with how it helps.

notes.b: The social function teaches children the norms (accepted ways of behaving), values and behaviour that allow them to live acceptably in society. This early learning at home is called primary socialisation.
points: Through observation, imitation and stimulation, children learn the norms, values, language, manners and behaviour that society accepts.
Consistent discipline and fair boundaries help children develop a set of values, self-control and respect for others, because they know what is expected.
Language, manners and social skills are learned at home before children enter school.

Schools continue socialisation (secondary socialisation) through the hidden curriculum, meaning the values and habits learned from school life rather than from lessons, and through SPHE. Peer groups, youth organisations, sports clubs and the media also continue it.

The State supports this function through schools and pre-schools and special provision. If a family fails to socialise a child, the State deals with non-conforming individuals through the justice system.
notes.tip: Describe socialisation, not social life: learning acceptable behaviour by imitation and observation, and consistent discipline. Do not confuse it with the emotional function.

notes.h: How institutions adopt or supplement functions
notes.b: The family does not carry out every function alone. Some institutions take a function over, and others help the family to carry it out.
points: To adopt a function is to take it over fully, for example foster care, residential care, boarding schools, and schools taking over formal teaching.
To supplement a function is to support the family in it, as in the examples given for each function above.
Over time, formal education, health care and many economic activities have moved out of the family, while the emotional and social functions remain mainly with the family.

Institutions that help include the State (HSE, Tusla, the Department of Social Protection, the Department of Education), schools, credit unions and banks, voluntary organisations, churches and community groups.
notes.tip: If asked how one function has been supplemented, choose one function, name an institution and say what it does, such as schools for the educational function. Lay out each answer as function, description, then State or institutional support.

notes.b: Sorting a week of ordinary family life into the five functions shows that one activity can serve more than one function.
points: Brainstorming: list each activity a family carries out in a week, then assign each one to a category.
Cooking a meal serves the physical function and also teaches table manners, which serves the social function.
Reading together serves the educational function and also the emotional function, by building closeness and confidence.
Paying bills and budgeting serve the economic function and teach children money management, which is part of the educational function.
Comforting a child is emotional, and teaching manners is social.

keyTerms.definition: The family's role in meeting the basic bodily needs of its members and protecting dependants.
The family's role in providing income and financial support for its dependants.
The family's role in giving love, security and a sense of belonging.
The family's role in passing on skills, language, values and customs and preparing children for formal schooling.
The family's role in teaching children the norms and behaviour that allow them to live acceptably in society.
The lifelong process by which a person learns the norms, values and behaviour of their society.
A person who relies on another for financial support, such as a child or an older person who cannot work.
The unwritten lessons pupils learn at school, such as punctuality, respect for authority and how to behave with peers.
The biological production of children, which ensures the continuation of the population.
An accepted standard of behaviour within a society or group.
A State scheme providing a free pre-school year for children before they start primary school.

questions.prompt: Explain how the State assists the family with one of its functions.
questions.model: One function named, for example the economic function, and one or two State supports explained: Child Benefit as a regular payment that helps with the cost of raising children, and the Working Family Payment for low-paid working families. Any other accurate State support for the chosen function, such as ECCE for the educational function or parenting programmes for the emotional function, with an explanation of how it helps.

questions.prompt: Discuss the functions of the family in society, explaining how other social institutions supplement or take over each function.
questions.model: Physical: the family provides food, warmth, shelter and clothing and protects dependants; supplemented by housing, GP and public health services and school meals. Economic: the family provides income and support for dependants and pays taxes that support the economy; supplemented by social welfare payments and MABS. Emotional: the family gives love, security and self-esteem; supplemented by counselling services and parenting programmes. Educational: the family is the primary educator, passing on skills and customs and supporting homework; supplemented by pre-school, schools and the ECCE scheme. Social: the family teaches norms, values and discipline through observation and imitation; supplemented by schools through the hidden curriculum, peer groups and, where the family fails, the judicial system. Conclusion of the answer: the family remains the core institution for every function, with other institutions sharing or taking over the functions when families cannot meet them.
